facts.claim: On tilt, players chased losses to restore a 'fair balance'.

facts.quote: a "house money effect" (increased risk seeking in the presence of a prior gain)
facts.claim: The house money effect is taking more risk after a gain.

facts.quote: "break-even effects" (in the presence of prior losses, outcomes which offer a chance to break even are especially attractive)
facts.claim: The break-even effect: after losses, a chance to get back to even is extra attractive.

facts.quote: This paper documents strong evidence for behavioral biases among Chicago Board of Trade proprietary traders
facts.claim: The study looked at professional Chicago Board of Trade traders.

facts.quote: Our traders appear highly loss-averse, regularly assuming above-average afternoon risk to recover from morning losses.
facts.claim: Pros who lost in the morning took above-average risk in the afternoon to recover.

facts.quote: In assessing his ability the trader takes too much credit for his successes. This leads him to become overconfident.
facts.claim: Taking too much credit for wins makes a trader overconfident.

facts.quote: Of 66,465 households with accounts at a large discount broker during 1991 to 1996, those that trade most earn an annual return of 11.4 percent, while the market returns 17.9 percent.
facts.claim: The heaviest-trading households earned 11.4% a year against the market's 17.9%.

facts.quote: Overconfidence can explain high trading levels and the resulting poor performance of individual investors.
facts.claim: Overconfidence explains heavy trading and poor results.

facts.quote: Revenge trading: Instead of reflecting on the loss and building a strong investment plan, the investor is motivated to take action for a quick gain.
facts.claim: Revenge trading is chasing a quick gain after a loss instead of reflecting.

facts.quote: In some cases, the second loss can be even larger than the first.
facts.claim: The revenge trade's loss can be bigger than the first.

facts.quote: Recency bias can prompt us to place undue importance on recent events. When we see our portfolio drop 10%, recency bias convinces us that it will just keep on dropping.
facts.claim: Recency bias gives recent events undue weight and says a drop will keep dropping.

facts.quote: During the 2008 financial crisis, many investors seemed to fall into the trap of recency bias.
facts.claim: Many investors fell into recency bias in 2008.

facts.quote: we hear ourselves say it over and over again: “I knew it all along.” The problem is that too often we actually didn’t know it all along, we only feel as though we did.
facts.claim: Hindsight bias is feeling you knew it all along when you didn't.

facts.quote: Ultimately, hindsight bias matters because it gets in the way of learning from our experiences.
facts.claim: Hindsight bias gets in the way of learning.

facts.quote: If you feel like you knew it all along, it means you won’t stop to examine why something really happened
facts.claim: If you think you knew it, you don't examine why it happened.

facts.quote: Hindsight bias can also make us overconfident in how certain we are about our own judgments.
facts.claim: Hindsight bias can make us overconfident.

facts.quote: The first level of hindsight bias, memory distortion, involves misremembering an earlier opinion or judgment (“I said it would happen”).
facts.claim: Hindsight bias starts with misremembering what you thought before.

facts.quote: The gambler’s fallacy is a belief in negative autocorrelation of a non-autocorrelated random sequence.
facts.claim: The gambler's fallacy expects a random run to reverse.

facts.quote: If he believes in the gambler’s fallacy, then after observing three heads his subjective probability of seeing another head is less than 50%. Thus he believes a tail is “due,”
facts.claim: After three heads, the believer thinks a fourth is less than 50% likely: a tail feels 'due'.

facts.quote: In contrast, the hot hand is a belief in positive autocorrelation of a non-autocorrelated random sequence.
facts.claim: The hot hand is the opposite belief: that a random run will continue.

facts.quote: At issue here is whether there is an outcome bias, in which people take outcomes into account in a way that is irrelevant to the true quality of the decision.
facts.claim: Outcome bias is letting the result color your view of the decision's quality.

facts.quote: Since good decisions can lead to bad outcomes (and vice versa) decision makers cannot infallibly be graded by their results.
facts.claim: Good decisions can turn out badly and bad ones well, so results alone can't grade a decision.

facts.quote: In poker you can win with the worst hand. You can lose with the best hand.
facts.claim: In poker you can win with the worst hand and lose with the best.

facts.quote: So if all I know is that Taylor and Morgan played poker for an hour and Taylor won, I know very little about the quality of the underlying decisions.
facts.claim: One win tells you little about the quality of the decisions.

facts.quote: That FOMO leads to overtrading, as the fear of missing leads to the taking of marginal trades.
facts.claim: FOMO leads to overtrading through marginal trades.

facts.quote: No matter how many opportunities I miss, ones always end up appearing later in the day or the next day.
facts.claim: Missed opportunities are always followed by new ones.

facts.quote: The goal is not to trade every possible opportunity, but to identify the best opportunities and trade those as well as possible.
facts.claim: Trade the best opportunities, not every one.

facts.quote: Our memories are biased by our emotions, as well as hindsight and the factors that most stick out in our mind.
facts.claim: Memory of our trades is biased by emotion and hindsight.

facts.quote: Hindsight bias occurs when people feel that they “knew it all along,” that is, when they believe that an event is more predictable after it becomes known than it was before it became known.
facts.claim: Hindsight bias is feeling you knew it all along: the event seems more predictable after it happens.

facts.quote: Consequences of hindsight bias include myopic attention to a single causal understanding of the past (to the neglect of other reasonable explanations) as well as general overconfidence in the certainty of one’s judgments.
facts.claim: Hindsight bias narrows how you explain the past and makes you overconfident in your judgments.

facts.quote: The evidence is most consistent with the law of small numbers and the gambler’s fallacy—people underestimating the likelihood of sequential streaks occurring by chance
facts.claim: The gambler's fallacy and the law of small numbers: people underestimate how often streaks happen by chance.

walkthroughs.title: Name it to catch it
steps: A research report done for the SEC says investors fall into predictable patterns. They make the same mistakes repeatedly.
Those patterns have names: FOMO, tilt, loss aversion, overconfidence and more. This unit teaches the names.
Mental game coach Jared Tendler puts it simply: you can't correct what you can't see. A name lets you see it.

walkthroughs.title: After a loss
steps: A loss stings more than an equal win feels good. That's loss aversion.
Anger can follow. Tendler calls that tilt: anger hurting your decisions.
Tilt can turn into revenge trading: bigger size and more trades, trying to win it back fast.
The fix is plain. Step away from the screen, cool off, then come back to your plan.

walkthroughs.title: After a win
steps: Wins set traps too. A trader who takes too much credit for wins grows overconfident.
Profits can feel like house money, so risk creeps up after a gain.
A short streak proves less than it feels. Keep your size tied to your rule, not your mood.

questions.q: In trading talk, what does FOMO stand for?
questions.why: Fear of missing out. FINRA's advice when FOMO grabs you: pause and evaluate before you act.
questions.lesson_line: FOMO is a feeling, not a setup. Feel it, then check your plan.

wrong.Fear of losing money: That's closer to loss aversion. FOMO is the fear of being left out of a move.
wrong.Following the crowd's trades: That's herding. FOMO often drives it, but FOMO names the fear itself.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The SEC's advice: stick with your long-term ___ and don't decide on a fear of missing out.
questions.why: Plan. The SEC's line is to stick with your long-term plan and not make decisions on a fear of missing out.
questions.lesson_line: The plan is the antidote. FOMO wants you to skip it.

questions.q: Which word names what you're feeling?
questions.story: A stock you watched broke out yesterday without you. Today it's up another 9%. Your chat is full of gains and you want in at any price.
questions.why: FOMO. FINRA's advice when excitement or FOMO takes hold is to pause and evaluate. Schwab warns that jumping on a move after it happened is a common mistake.
questions.lesson_line: If you missed the entry, you missed it. Wait for the next setup.

wrong.Tilt: Tilt is anger, usually after losses. This is the itch of being left out.
wrong.Anchoring: Anchoring is leaning on a first number, like an old price. Nothing here hangs on a reference price.
wrong.Loss aversion: Loss aversion is the sting of losing. You haven't lost anything here; you're afraid of missing out.

questions.q: Pump-and-dump scammers count on your FOMO to get you to buy fast.
questions.why: True. FINRA says pump-and-dump operators rely on FOMO, and they press you to act immediately or 'never get another chance'.
questions.lesson_line: A tip that says buy now or never is a red flag, not a setup.

questions.q: What's your move?
questions.story: A stock on your list breaks out on big volume while you're away. Two days later it's far past your entry. A friend says it's not too late.
choices: Let it go and wait for a new setup
Buy now at double size to catch up
Buy now, strong stocks keep going
questions.answer: Let it go and wait for a new setup
questions.why: Let it go and wait for a new setup. The SEC says to stick with your plan and not decide on a fear of missing out. Steenbarger: the goal is the best opportunities, not every one.
questions.lesson_line: There's always another setup. Wait for one you can plan.

wrong.Buy now at double size to catch up: That's FOMO setting your size. Being late doesn't change your sizing rule.
wrong.Buy now, strong stocks keep going: Some do. But your plan's entry is gone, and Schwab warns a late entry can come right before a reversal.

questions.q: In trading, what does it mean to be on tilt?
choices: Making bad decisions out of anger
Feeling too sure after a few wins
Holding a losing trade too long
questions.answer: Making bad decisions out of anger
questions.why: Making bad decisions out of anger. Tendler calls tilt a problem with anger in performance. A poker study defines it as out-of-control decisions driven by negative emotions.
questions.lesson_line: Tilt is anger placing your trades. Spot it early and step away.

wrong.Feeling too sure after a few wins: That's overconfidence. Tendler says no one gets angry about winning.
wrong.Holding a losing trade too long: That's the disposition effect. Tilt is about anger driving your decisions.

questions.q: Tilt is often set off by a big loss.
questions.why: True. A study of poker players' own stories found tilt was often set off by a significant loss. Tendler ties drawdown anger to triggers piling up faster than you can recover.
questions.lesson_line: After a big loss, check your temper before the next click.

questions.q: Which word names the state you're in?
questions.story: You get stopped out twice before noon. You're furious at the market. You jump straight back in with no setup.
questions.why: Tilt. Anger is driving the trade. Tendler's own example is jumping back into a position after getting stopped out for the second time.
questions.lesson_line: Two stop-outs and a hot temper is the moment to stop, not to press.

wrong.FOMO: FOMO is the fear of missing a move. Here it's anger at the losses pushing you.
wrong.Anchoring: Anchoring is fixing on a first number. Nothing here hangs on a reference price.
wrong.Hindsight bias: Hindsight bias is 'I knew it all along' after the fact. This is anger in the moment.

questions.q: By Tendler's definition, feeling unbeatable after a run of winners is a form of tilt.
questions.why: False. Tilt is anger. Tendler says no one gets angry about winning, and calls that problem overconfidence or fear. The poker research ties tilt to negative emotions.
questions.lesson_line: Name it right to fix it. Anger after losses is tilt; swagger after wins is overconfidence.

questions.q: What is revenge trading?
choices: Trading to win back a loss fast
Selling a stock that let you down
questions.answer: Trading to win back a loss fast
questions.why: Trading to win back a loss fast. CIBC describes acting for a quick gain instead of reflecting on the loss. Investopedia: seeking revenge on the market with bigger, more frequent trades.
questions.lesson_line: A loss is a cost of doing business. Chasing it back today can turn it into two.

wrong.Re-entering after a stop-out: Re-entering on a fresh, planned setup is normal. Revenge is about getting the money back.
wrong.Selling a stock that let you down: Selling a loser can be the right move. Revenge trading is the next trade, made to win the money back.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Alan Farley's rule: don't make up for a losing trade by trading more. ___ trading is a recipe for disaster.
questions.why: Revenge. Investopedia's list of professional rules says so plainly, and Schwab ties revenge trading to many trading blowups.
questions.lesson_line: Trading more to make up a loss is the trap. Fewer, better trades get you back.

questions.q: Revenge trading usually shows up as smaller size and fewer trades.
questions.why: False. Investopedia says traders out for revenge usually increase the size and frequency of their trades. Schwab names doubling down on the next trade to make up the loss.
questions.lesson_line: If your size jumps right after a loss, that's revenge, not conviction.

questions.q: What's the better move?
questions.story: It's 11 a.m. You're down 3R on three stop-outs. A so-so setup shows up, and you feel the urge to go double size and make it all back.
choices: Take it and skip the stop
questions.why: Step away and cool off. Schwab says the first thing to do after a big loss is step away, and suggests a pledge to stop for the day after a set loss.
questions.lesson_line: Set a daily loss limit before the open. When it hits, you're done for the day.

wrong.Take it at double size: That's revenge trading: bigger size right after losses. CIBC warns the second loss can be bigger than the first.
wrong.Take it and skip the stop: Pulling a stop is often a way to avoid admitting you were wrong. It turns a planned loss into an open one.
wrong.Short it to get even: Schwab lists trading against a stock 'to get even with the market' as an emotional mistake.

questions.q: You take a dozen trades a day, most of them marginal, and costs pile up. Which word fits?
questions.why: Overtrading. Investopedia defines it as excessive buying and selling that raises costs and hurts results. Steenbarger ties it to taking marginal trades.
questions.lesson_line: Every trade should earn its place. If it's a maybe, it's a no.

wrong.Scaling in: Scaling in is building one position in planned portions. It isn't a pile of marginal trades.
wrong.Diversifying: Diversifying spreads risk across holdings on purpose. Overtrading is excess activity.

questions.q: Barber and Odean: the heaviest traders earned 11.4% a year and the market 17.9%. How many points a year did they trail by?
questions.why: 6.5 points. That's 17.9 minus 11.4. Barber and Odean say overconfidence can explain the heavy trading and the poor results.
questions.lesson_line: Activity isn't edge. The busiest traders in that study trailed the market.

questions.q: What is overconfidence bias?
choices: Being sure you saw the outcome coming
Following the crowd into a hot name
questions.why: Overrating your own skill and knowledge. Schwab defines it as overestimating your knowledge and abilities, which tricks you into risky bets.
questions.lesson_line: Let your record, not your mood, tell you how good you are.

wrong.Being sure you saw the outcome coming: That's hindsight bias, though it can feed overconfidence.
wrong.Following the crowd into a hot name: That's herding. Overconfidence is about how you rate yourself.

questions.q: Research ties overconfidence to trading too often.
questions.why: True. A Library of Congress report done for the SEC says active trading correlates with overconfidence. Barber and Odean say overconfidence can explain high trading levels.
questions.lesson_line: When you start trading more because you feel sharp, slow down.

questions.q: Which word fits best?
questions.story: You've hit five winners in a row. You decide you've figured this market out. You triple your normal size on the next trade.
questions.why: Overconfidence. Gervais and Odean show a trader who takes too much credit for wins becomes overconfident. A short run proves much less than it feels.
questions.lesson_line: Keep size tied to your risk rule, not to your streak.

wrong.Loss aversion: Loss aversion is fear of losses. Here you're ignoring risk, not fearing it.
wrong.Anchoring: Anchoring is leaning on a first number. Nothing here hangs on a reference price.
wrong.Familiarity bias: Familiarity bias favors names you know. This is about how you rate your own skill.

questions.q: FINRA Foundation research found social media users less often overrate their investing knowledge.
questions.why: False. FINRA says social media users are more likely than non-users to show overconfidence in their investment knowledge.
questions.lesson_line: A feed full of winners makes everyone feel smart. Check your own numbers.

questions.q: Which word is this: wins are my skill, losses are bad luck?
questions.why: Self-attribution bias. Schwab defines it as crediting wins to your skill and blaming losses on outside forces. The SEC's report links it to overconfidence.
questions.lesson_line: Grade wins as hard as losses. Luck shows up on both sides.

wrong.Hindsight bias: Hindsight bias is believing an outcome was predictable after it happened.
wrong.Confirmation bias: Confirmation bias is favoring information that backs what you already think.
wrong.Outcome bias: Outcome bias is judging a decision by its result. Self-attribution is about who gets the credit.

questions.q: Where does this habit tend to lead?
questions.story: You review your journal. Every winner is tagged 'great read.' Every loser is tagged 'bad luck' or 'market was rigged.'
choices: A truer read of your edge
questions.why: Overconfidence, then bigger bets. Gervais and Odean show a trader who takes too much credit for wins becomes overconfident. Schwab names this habit self-attribution bias.
questions.lesson_line: Tag the real cause of every loss. 'Bad luck' is a tag you earn, not a default.

wrong.More careful position sizing: The opposite. Taking credit for every win makes you feel safer than you are.
wrong.A truer read of your edge: It hides your edge. Blaming luck for losses keeps you from fixing them.

questions.q: What is loss aversion?
choices: A loss hurts more than an equal gain
Avoiding risk to protect your capital
Selling your winners far too early
questions.answer: A loss hurts more than an equal gain
questions.why: A loss stings more than a same-size gain. The Nobel summary of Kahneman's work: most people are more averse to losses than partial to gains of the same size.
questions.lesson_line: Expect a loss to hurt more than a win feels good. Plan your exit before that feeling shows up.

wrong.Avoiding risk to protect your capital: That's risk aversion, which can be rational. Loss aversion is the lopsided feeling about losses and gains.
wrong.Selling your winners far too early: That's half of the disposition effect, which loss aversion helps explain.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Kahneman and Tversky's ___ theory says people weigh losses more heavily than equal gains.
questions.why: Prospect. A Library of Congress report done for the SEC calls prospect theory one of the foundations of behavioral finance.
questions.lesson_line: Prospect theory is the science behind 'losses hurt more.'

questions.q: Loss aversion only ever makes people more careful.
questions.why: False. Schwab says loss aversion can also push you to take extra risk when you're down. The OSC says the pain of losing can increase risk-taking.
questions.lesson_line: Down money, you may want to swing bigger. That's the bias talking.

questions.q: Which bias is at work?
questions.story: Your stock falls through your stop. Selling would make the loss real, so you cancel the stop and wait to get back to even.
questions.why: Loss aversion. Schwab says once shares fall below your cost, selling means taking a loss, so you hold, and that can make the loss worse.
questions.lesson_line: You set the stop when you were calm. Trust that version of you.

wrong.FOMO: FOMO is about missing a move. This is about refusing to take a loss.
wrong.Herd mentality: Herding is copying others. Nobody else is in this decision.
wrong.Recency bias: Recency bias overweights what just happened. The pull here is the pain of booking a loss.

questions.q: What is the disposition effect?
choices: Adding to a stock that keeps falling
questions.why: Selling winners early, holding losers. The SEC calls it holding losing investments too long and selling winning investments too soon.
questions.lesson_line: Cut losers fast and let winners work. The bias pulls you the other way.

wrong.Adding to a stock that keeps falling: That's adding to a loser. Related habit, but the disposition effect is about which positions you sell.
wrong.Selling everything in a panic: That's panic selling. The disposition effect is quieter: you cut winners and keep losers.

questions.q: Per the SEC, winners people sell too soon often go on to trail the losers they keep.
questions.why: False. The SEC bulletin says the winners sold often keep outperforming the losers still held. The report behind it says the habit achieves the reverse of what investors hope.
questions.lesson_line: Let the chart and the plan decide what you sell, not where you bought it.

questions.q: Which word fits?
questions.story: You need cash. Stock A is up 18% and acting well. Stock B is down 12% and below its stop. You sell A and keep B until it comes back.
questions.why: Disposition effect. Selling the winner and keeping the loser is exactly the pattern the SEC describes. Schwab's test: if you wouldn't buy B today, it may be time to sell.
questions.lesson_line: When you need cash, sell what's broken first. B broke your stop.

wrong.House money effect: House money is taking more risk with recent profits. This is about which position you sell.
wrong.Familiarity bias: Familiarity bias favors names you know. Both of these are names you know.
wrong.Hindsight bias: Hindsight bias is 'I knew it' after the fact. This is a choice you're making now.

questions.q: What is confirmation bias?
choices: Favoring info that backs what you think
Waiting for price to confirm a breakout
Believing you knew it all along
questions.answer: Favoring info that backs what you think
questions.why: Favoring info that backs what you think. Schwab defines it as favoring information that supports your beliefs while ignoring contradictory evidence.
questions.lesson_line: Before you buy, write the bear case. If you can't, you haven't looked.

wrong.Waiting for price to confirm a breakout: That's price confirmation, a chart habit. The bias is about filtering information to fit your view.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Schwab's fix for confirmation bias: seek out reputable views that ___ your own.
questions.why: Contradict. Schwab says if you can't rebut the opposing view with data, bias may be blinding you. Investopedia says to seek ideas that challenge your view.
questions.lesson_line: Read the best case against your trade. If you can't answer it, you're not ready.

questions.q: Which word names this?
questions.story: You own a stock. You follow five accounts that love it. You mute the one account that keeps posting the bear case.
questions.why: Confirmation bias. Schwab's own example is seeking more from the voices that agree with you, the tendency to seek information that supports what you already believe.
questions.lesson_line: Keep one smart bear in your feed. Muting them doesn't make the risk go away.

wrong.Herd mentality: Herding is copying what others do. Here you're choosing which opinions you hear.
wrong.Anchoring: Anchoring is leaning on a first number. This is about filtering opinions.
wrong.Gambler's fallacy: The gambler's fallacy expects a streak to reverse. Nothing here is about a streak.

questions.q: Confirmation bias can keep you in a losing view after the evidence turns.
questions.why: True. Schwab's example is a trader who ignores negative news and refuses to sell as the stock trends lower. Investopedia says it keeps bulls bullish whatever the market does.
questions.lesson_line: Your thesis can be wrong. Let your stop, not your reading list, decide.

questions.q: What is anchoring?
choices: Leaning on the first number you saw
Holding a stock for the long run
Following a mentor into every trade
questions.answer: Leaning on the first number you saw
questions.why: Over-relying on the first number you saw. The OSC defines anchoring as relying too heavily on the first piece of information you're offered.
questions.lesson_line: Ask what the stock is doing now, not what it used to cost.

wrong.Holding a stock for the long run: That's a holding period. Anchoring is a reference number steering your judgment.
wrong.Following a mentor into every trade: That's closer to herding. Anchoring is about a number in your head.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: You bought at $50. It's $42 and below your stop, but you won't sell under $50. That $50 is acting as an ___.
questions.why: Anchor. The OSC says refusing to sell below what you paid comes from loss aversion and the original price acting as an anchor: a first number that becomes an unintended reference point.
questions.lesson_line: Your entry price means nothing to the stock. Judge it as it is now.

questions.q: Which word fits?
questions.story: A stock fell from $200 to $120 over a year. You buy it because it used to be $200, so it must be cheap. The trend is still down.
questions.why: Anchoring. Schwab's example is fixing on a stock's historical price. The OSC compares it to a crossed-out price tag that makes the sale price feel cheap.
questions.lesson_line: An old high is history, not a target.

wrong.FOMO: FOMO is fear of missing a move. Nothing here is moving away from you.
wrong.Herd mentality: Herding is copying others. This is your own reference price at work.
wrong.Hindsight bias: Hindsight bias is 'I knew it all along' after the fact. This is about a past price.

questions.q: A number can sway your judgment even when it has nothing to do with the trade.
questions.why: True. The OSC says an anchor can still influence you when it's completely irrelevant. Schwab says we fixate on the first data point whether it's relevant or not.
questions.lesson_line: Notice the first number you saw. Then ask if it should matter at all.

questions.q: What is recency bias?
choices: Believing a streak must end soon
Judging a trade by its result
questions.why: Overweighting what just happened. Schwab calls it over-emphasizing what's top of mind. Morningstar says it gives recent events undue importance.
questions.lesson_line: One rough month is one month. Judge setups on the full record.

questions.q: Which bias may be steering you?
questions.story: The market dropped hard last month. Now every bounce looks like a trap to you. A strong new leader breaks out and you pass without even looking.
questions.why: Recency bias. Morningstar says that after a drop, recency bias convinces us it will keep on dropping. Schwab gives the same case after a recent plunge.
questions.lesson_line: Judge each setup on its own chart, not on how last month felt.

wrong.FOMO: FOMO would push you in. This is the opposite: fear from the last drop keeping you out.
wrong.House money effect: House money is taking more risk after gains. You're taking less after losses.
wrong.Familiarity bias: Familiarity bias favors names you know. This is about the last month's memory.

questions.q: In the 2008 crisis, recency bias led many investors out of stocks before the recovery.
questions.why: True. Investopedia says the 2008 and 2009 crisis led many investors to exit stocks, and the market bounced back in the years after. Morningstar ties that era to recency bias.
questions.lesson_line: The last crash feels like the next one. Let price, not memory, bring you back.

questions.q: One stock's 30% earnings gap-down is all over the news. Now every earnings report feels like a disaster. Which bias?
questions.why: Availability bias. The OSC says we judge by readily available information, and the more dramatic the recent event, the more it sways us. Schwab calls it the availability heuristic.
questions.lesson_line: One vivid story isn't the odds. Check how often it really happens.

wrong.Anchoring: Anchoring is leaning on a first number. Here a vivid story is setting your odds.
wrong.Confirmation bias: Confirmation bias is filtering for what you already believe. This is one dramatic event looming large.
wrong.House money effect: House money is taking more risk with profits. Nothing here is about gains.

questions.q: What is hindsight bias?
choices: Feeling you knew it all along
Seeing a pattern in a random run
questions.answer: Feeling you knew it all along
questions.why: Feeling you knew it all along. Roese and Vohs describe it as believing an event was more predictable after it happened than before.
questions.lesson_line: If you really knew it, it would be in your plan from before.

wrong.Studying your past trades: Reviewing trades is a good habit. Hindsight bias is what distorts the review.
wrong.Seeing a pattern in a random run: That's trusting a small sample, the 'law of small numbers'. Hindsight bias is the past looking predictable.

questions.q: Hindsight bias makes it harder to learn from your trades.
questions.why: True. The APS says hindsight bias gets in the way of learning: if you feel you knew it all along, you won't examine why it happened. Steenbarger adds that hindsight bends our memory of trades.
questions.lesson_line: Write the plan before the trade. Then the review has something honest to check.

questions.q: Hindsight bias can feed overconfidence.
questions.why: True. The APS says it can make us overconfident about our own judgments. Roese and Vohs list general overconfidence among its consequences.
questions.lesson_line: 'I saw that coming' builds false confidence. Your written record keeps you honest.

questions.q: What best protects you from this?
questions.story: You passed on a stock last month. It has since run 60%. Now you tell everyone the move was obvious and you saw it coming.
choices: Write down your read at the time
Buy it now to make up for the miss
Forget it and move on quickly
questions.answer: Write down your read at the time
questions.why: Write down your read at the time. Roese and Vohs say hindsight bias starts with misremembering what you thought before. Steenbarger notes that memory is biased by emotion and hindsight.
questions.lesson_line: Memory edits itself. A note written at the time doesn't.

wrong.Buy it now to make up for the miss: That's FOMO and regret steering you. Missing the move doesn't make it a setup now.
wrong.Forget it and move on quickly: Moving on is fine, but the illusion repeats. A written record shows what you really thought.

questions.q: What is herd mentality?
choices: Copying others over your own research
Investing in a company everyone knows
Trusting a stock's old high price
questions.answer: Copying others over your own research
questions.why: Copying others instead of your own work. The OSC says herding is doing the same thing because others are doing it. Schwab says chasing trends outsources your due diligence to the crowd.
questions.lesson_line: A crowded trade can still be a good trade. Just make sure it's your trade.

wrong.Investing in a company everyone knows: Favoring well-known names is familiarity bias.
wrong.Trusting a stock's old high price: That's anchoring. Herding is copying the crowd instead of doing your own work.

questions.q: Herding can help feed bubbles and crashes.
questions.why: True. Investopedia ties bubbles to herd behavior and calls herding a cause of dramatic rallies and sell-offs. The OSC says following others can push us to buy or sell out of panic.
questions.lesson_line: In a stampede, stick to your stops and your size.

questions.q: Buying a popular stock on your own plan, with your stop set, is herding just because others own it.
questions.why: False. Herding is doing something because others are doing it, instead of relying on your own analysis. Owning what others own isn't the bias; skipping your own work is.
questions.lesson_line: Popular isn't the problem. Not knowing why you're in is.

questions.q: What is the house money effect?
questions.why: Taking more risk with recent profits. Thaler and Johnson found more risk seeking after a prior gain. Investopedia calls it risking profits more freely than earned money.
questions.lesson_line: Profit is your money once it's booked. Risk it by the same rule.

wrong.Trading with someone else's capital: That's trading other people's money. The effect is about how you treat your own recent gains.
wrong.Keeping recent profits in cash: That's the opposite: locking gains away rather than risking them.

questions.q: Which word fits?
questions.story: You're up big on the month. You tell yourself it's not really your money yet. You take your next trade at three times your normal risk.
questions.why: House money effect. Investopedia says people take more risk with profits than with earned money, and it comes from mental accounting. Thaler and Johnson found the same after a prior gain.
questions.lesson_line: Keep risk per trade tied to your account, not to how the month is going.

wrong.Loss aversion: Loss aversion makes losses loom large. Here a gain is making risk feel small.
wrong.Disposition effect: The disposition effect is selling winners and keeping losers. This is about sizing up after gains.
wrong.Anchoring: Anchoring is leaning on a first number. This is about treating profit as free money.

questions.q: Down on the day, you take a long-shot trade because it could get you back to even. Which word is this?
questions.why: Break-even effect. Thaler and Johnson found that after losses, a chance to break even looks especially attractive. Schwab says fear of locking in a loss can drive riskier decisions.
questions.lesson_line: Getting back to even is not a setup. Grade the trade as if you were flat.

wrong.House money effect: That's the flip side: more risk after a gain.
wrong.Disposition effect: That's selling winners and holding losers. This is reaching for a long shot to get even.

questions.q: Chicago Board of Trade pros who lost in the morning tended to cut their risk in the afternoon.
questions.why: False. Coval and Shumway found Chicago Board of Trade pros who lost in the morning took above-average risk in the afternoon to recover.
questions.lesson_line: Pros feel it too. A daily loss limit protects you from your afternoon self.

questions.q: What is the gambler's fallacy?
choices: Thinking a streak is 'due' to end
Believing a hot streak will continue
Betting big when you have an edge
questions.answer: Thinking a streak is 'due' to end
questions.why: Thinking a streak is 'due' to end. Croson and Sundali define it as expecting a random run to reverse, so the other outcome feels 'due'.
questions.lesson_line: The next trade doesn't know about the last few.

wrong.Believing a hot streak will continue: That's the opposite belief, called the hot hand.
wrong.Betting big when you have an edge: That's a sizing choice, not this fallacy. The fallacy is about expecting a run to reverse.

questions.q: Which word fits that reasoning?
questions.story: Your tested setup has lost five times in a row. You double your size on the next one because a win is due.
questions.why: Gambler's fallacy. Croson and Sundali define it as expecting a random run to reverse, so a win feels 'due'. Schwab adds that a losing streak can flag a real problem.
questions.lesson_line: Never size up because a win feels due. After a losing run, check for a problem and trade smaller.

wrong.Hindsight bias: Hindsight bias is 'I knew it' after the fact. This is a prediction about the next trade.
wrong.Anchoring: Anchoring is leaning on a first number. This is about expecting a streak to flip.
wrong.Familiarity bias: Familiarity bias favors names you know. This is about streaks and odds.

questions.q: What is outcome bias?
choices: Judging a decision by how it turned out
Crediting wins to skill, losses to luck
Expecting a trend to keep going
questions.answer: Judging a decision by how it turned out
questions.why: Judging a decision by how it turned out. Baron and Hershey describe letting outcomes count in a way that's irrelevant to the decision's true quality.
questions.lesson_line: Grade the decision and the result separately. They're two different grades.

wrong.Expecting a trend to keep going: That's a view on the market. Outcome bias is about how you grade decisions.
wrong.Crediting wins to skill, losses to luck: That's self-attribution bias. Outcome bias is grading the decision by its result.

questions.q: How should you grade that trade?
questions.story: You chased a gap with no stop and no plan. It ran, and you made 4R on the trade.
questions.why: Bad decision, lucky result. Good decisions can lead to bad outcomes and the reverse, so results alone can't grade a decision. Annie Duke: in poker you can win with the worst hand.
questions.lesson_line: A win that broke your rules is still a mistake. Tag it, or you'll repeat it.

wrong.Great trade, do it again: That's outcome bias. Repeat it and one day the missing stop costs you.
wrong.Good decision, since it paid: The payout doesn't make the decision good. Baron and Hershey call that outcome bias.

questions.q: What is familiarity bias?
questions.why: Favoring familiar, well-known names. The SEC says it covers your own country or company and popular 'glamour' investments, and it can leave you under-diversified.
questions.lesson_line: Knowing the product isn't knowing the stock.

wrong.Trading only setups you've tested: That's discipline, not a bias. The bias is about which names feel safe because they're familiar.

questions.q: What is mental accounting?
choices: Treating money by where it came from
Tracking every trade in a journal
Doing quick trade math in your head
questions.answer: Treating money by where it came from
questions.why: Treating money by where it came from. The OSC says people treat money differently by how they got it or plan to spend it. Investopedia says it's behind the house money effect.
questions.lesson_line: A dollar of profit is a dollar. Risk it by the same rule as the rest.

wrong.Tracking every trade in a journal: That's record keeping, a good habit.
wrong.Doing quick trade math in your head: That's mental math. Mental accounting is about how you label money.

questions.q: Five winners in your first six trades proves a new setup has an edge.
questions.why: False. Six trades is a tiny sample. Kahneman's work describes a 'law of small numbers': people treat small samples as if they told the whole story.
questions.lesson_line: Keep size small until the sample is big. A few trades can't tell skill from luck.

questions.q: What's wrong with that conclusion?
questions.story: A newsletter's picks beat the index two years in a row. A friend says that proves the editor is a genius.
choices: Two years is too small a sample
questions.answer: Two years is too small a sample
questions.why: Two years is too small a sample. The Nobel summary of Kahneman's work uses nearly this case, a fund manager beating the index two years running: the evidence is much weaker than it feels.
questions.lesson_line: Small samples flatter. Judge a guru, or a setup, on many trades.

wrong.Beating the index is easy: It isn't. The point is that two years can't separate skill from luck.
wrong.Newsletters can't pick stocks: Some may. You just can't tell from two years.

questions.q: In market terms, what is a mania?
choices: A fast rise on crowd enthusiasm
A stock up on strong earnings
questions.answer: A fast rise on crowd enthusiasm
questions.why: A fast rise on crowd enthusiasm. The SEC calls a mania, or bubble, a rapid rise driven by collective exuberance, usually followed by a panic of wide-scale selling.
questions.lesson_line: Manias usually end in panics. Keep your stop in place on the way up.

wrong.A long, steady uptrend: A steady trend isn't a mania by itself. The SEC's word is about a rapid rise on collective enthusiasm.
wrong.A stock up on strong earnings: That's a move on results. A mania is driven by crowd excitement.

conflicts: Loss aversion size: Schwab and the OSC say a loss feels about twice (OSC: twice) as strong as an equal gain; Investopedia says some studies suggest about twice but others question whether loss aversion exists or matters in practice (f77). No question keys a multiple; every key says only that losses weigh more than equal gains, which the SEC report, Nobel summary, Fidelity and Investopedia all state.

Self-attribution bias: Schwab defines it as crediting wins to skill and losses to outside forces (f44), and Gervais and Odean describe a trader taking too much credit for successes (f120); Investopedia's behavioral finance page defines self-attribution as choices based on overconfidence in one's own skill. The SEC report pairs the two ('overconfidence (self-attribution bias)'). Questions use the Schwab definition, which the paper supports.

Recency vs availability: Investopedia treats them as one bias ('also known as recency bias or availability bias', f79); Schwab and the OSC describe availability as its own shortcut. q37-q39 key recency bias and q40 keys availability bias; no question lists both as choices.

Tilt: poker players use the word loosely. Tendler (f108, f110) restricts it to anger and says 'winner's tilt' is overconfidence or fear; the poker study (f113) says negative emotions. Questions follow that narrow meaning.

The same behavior has several names: holding a loser below the stop is described as loss aversion (Schwab f42), the disposition effect (SEC f01), the original price acting as an anchor (OSC f153, which names loss aversion and the anchor together; Investopedia f83 files judging by the entry price under disposition bias) and the break-even effect (Thaler and Johnson f117). Each question's choices include only one of these, so only one key fits.

Not used: the SEC's Library of Congress report quotes Mohacsy and Lefer calling momentum investing a manifestation of magical thinking and herd behavior. That is one cited opinion about a widely studied strategy, so no question says trend or momentum trading is herding; q47 teaches herding as copying others instead of doing your own work.

Gambler's fallacy: the formal definition (f131, f148) is about independent random events. Trade outcomes are not perfectly independent, so q53 keys only the reasoning 'a win is due after a losing run', which no source supports, and never claims trade outcomes are random.
